answer.answer: The win condition is met, but the study does not answer the question it was set. Five settings on five different scenes are confirmed as challenging: S1 (048b974e), S2 (07981e6a), S5 (0d4893f5), S10 (18d28973) and S12 (1bbe02fc). All five are at the nominal setting (1.0x speed, 0 s shift), and the triage shows that none of the failures involve the pedestrian. The policy ignored a right-turn route, drifted or turned left, and then hit parked, oncoming or adjacent vehicles or left the road. So these scenes fail on their own, not because of speed or timing. Only two non-nominal settings were run (0.6x and 0.8x on 12a09194, one run each, no failures), and no step-out time other than 0 s was tried, so no speed–timing combination has been shown to cause a failure. Three runs per setting put each confirmed rate somewhere between just above one half and certain. S12's failures may be partly a map-boundary artifact, and every S1 and S10 failure was flagged as a possible simulator artifact.

findings.claim: All five confirmed settings fail at the nominal 1.0x speed and 0 s step-out. Their failures come from the scene and the policy, not from varying speed or pedestrian timing.

None of the triaged failures is a pedestrian collision. The ego turned left against a RIGHT route command into a stopped vehicle (048b974e), drifted left along parked cars into parked car 6 (07981e6a), yawed into the car alongside in the left lane (0d4893f5), or drove onto the left median (18d28973).

On 1bbe02fc, every failure is an offroad flag at the stop line with the ego only about half a metre from the human path, while the route command still read STRAIGHT. Triage could not assign blame, so this confirmed case may be partly a map-boundary artifact.

Every S1 and S10 failure was flagged as a possible artifact (more than 3.5 m off the recorded path or black frames). Triage still reads them as policy errors: a wrong-way turn and driving onto the median with a clean camera view. So the flag most likely reflects the policy leaving the path, not rendering.
0caa8f1a also fails at nominal, with the ego crossing the double yellow head-on into oncoming car 85, but it was not repeated enough to be confirmed.

The cleaner scenes (0b10bce8, 0e002edd, 18f8dbd6) did not fail at nominal, and neither did 12a09194 at 0.6x, 0.8x or 1.0x. These are the scenes where a speed–timing effect could actually be measured, and they were barely explored. 12a09194 has only one run at each speed, which is a hint, not a rate.

open: Whether any combination of ego speed (0.6x–1.4x) and pedestrian step-out shift (±2 s) causes a failure: no non-zero shift and no speed above 1.0x was run. The study stopped once the nominal failures filled the top 5. Settle this by spending the rest of the budget (about 20 runs) on the speed × shift grid on 0e002edd, 18f8dbd6 and 0b10bce8, e.g. 1.2x and 1.4x crossed with -1 s, 0 s and +1 s, then repeating any failure or close approach 3–5 times.

Whether the policy ever hits the pedestrian at all: the failure check cannot tell which actor was hit, and no triaged failure involved a person. Settle this with the grid above plus a pedestrian-specific closest-approach check.
Whether 1bbe02fc (S12) is a real failure or a map-boundary artifact: check the lane-boundary geometry at its stop line, or rerun with an offroad tolerance.
Whether 0caa8f1a (S4) fails reliably at nominal: 2–3 more repeats would settle it.

Whether the nominal-failure scenes are worth keeping for this question at all: they fail on route-following before pedestrian timing can matter. Swapping them out of the top-5 for speed–timing cases on the clean scenes would answer the brief as it was meant.
